messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 62

He is a sixty-seven-year-old man who has managed the same downtown hotel for thirty-two years. When I first met him, he sat rigidly in the armchair, hands folded in his lap, eyes scanning my office as if cataloging every exit. He spoke in clipped sentences, apologizing for taking up my time. “I’m not the type to complain,” he said. “But my wife said I had to come.”

The robbery happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday night in late February. He had stayed late to reconcile the nightly receipts, a routine he had performed thousands of times. The hotel was quiet, the lobby empty except for the night clerk. He was walking across the underground parking garage toward his car when two men stepped out from behind a concrete pillar. One held a knife. The other had a gun, or something that looked like a gun—he still cannot say for certain. They demanded his wallet, his watch, the cash bag he was carrying. He gave them everything. They shoved him to the ground, and one of them kicked him in the ribs. Then they were gone.

He remembers lying on the cold concrete, staring at the ceiling lights, waiting for someone to find him. The night clerk found him ten minutes later. He refused an ambulance. He drove himself home, walked into the kitchen, and told his wife he had been mugged. He did not cry. He did not raise his voice. He showered, went to bed, and woke up the next morning to go back to work.

In the weeks that followed, he began to change. The parking garage became a battlefield. He now parks three blocks away in a surface lot, even in rain or snow, because he cannot bear the echo of his own footsteps on concrete. He walks to his car with his keys gripped between his fingers, and he checks the back seat before he gets in. He refuses to carry a cash bag after dark. He has asked the night clerk to walk him out, though the clerk is twenty-three and weighs less than he does. He knows this is irrational. He does it anyway.

At the hotel, he has become short-tempered. A guest complaint about a noisy air conditioner sent him into a silent rage that lasted an hour. He avoids the underground floor entirely, taking the stairs three flights up to avoid the elevator that stops there. He has stopped attending the monthly managers’ dinner because it ends late, and the walk to the car feels too exposed.

At home, his wife says he is not himself. He wakes at 3:00 a.m. most nights, certain he heard a door open. He lies still, listening, his heart pounding so hard he can feel it in his throat. He has stopped watching crime dramas, stopped going to the grocery store after dark. He no longer jokes with the front desk staff the way he used to. He feels hollow, as if something inside him was taken that night and never returned.

He told me, with a tight smile, “I used to be the guy who handled emergencies. Now I’m the guy who can’t handle a parking lot.” He avoids talking about the event. When his wife brings it up, he changes the subject. When I ask him to describe the feeling of lying on the concrete, he pauses for twenty seconds and then says, “I don’t remember much.” But his hands are shaking.

He scored 62 on the PCL-5, endorsing every hyperarousal item and nearly all the avoidance and intrusion items. He does not see himself as traumatized. He sees himself as weak. He wants to go back to the man he was before—the one who walked through that garage without thinking twice. But every night, when the parking lot lights flicker, he is still on the ground, staring up at the fluorescence, waiting for someone to find him.
